Paragraph: While living in exile in the forest, Queen Draupadi expressed deep frustration and despair to Yudhisthira, questioning why righteous people suffer while the wicked thrive. Yudhisthira gently replied: 'I do not practice Dharma for reward, O Queen. I practice Dharma because it is right. Perform your duties with a calm heart, without letting bitterness poison your spirit.'
Situation/Problem_Faced: Resentment, existential anger, loss of faith due to injustice, and chronic stress.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Yudhisthira reframes morality, teaching that doing good is its own intrinsic reward and warning against letting bitterness take root.
Outcome/Resolution: Draupadi finds the emotional endurance needed to sustain her resolve through the long years of exile.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.Feelings of Hopelessness: Existential doubt, Loss of faith in justice

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Dharma-Hetuta (Practicing virtue for its own sake, not for gain)
Nir-vairata (Refusing to let anger turn into chronic bitterness)
Dhairya (Steadfast moral endurance in adverse conditions)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Virtue should be practiced for its own intrinsic good, not as a transaction for smooth circumstances.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Helps resolve moral injury, resentment, and existential anger through intrinsic value alignment.
